DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
The case for raising the weekend rate is reasonable. The case the paper actually makes is not: its main piece of evidence is a seasonal effect, the revenue figure uses the wrong room count and assumes every room sells at the rate being raised, and the two-night minimum is aimed at the wedding guests who make up 38% of Saturday bookings.

## What holds up

- **Arithmetic.** 2025 weekend occupancy averages 79.2% ✓. 124 × 104 × 0.79 × £20 = £203,758 ✓.
- **Competitor gap.** A £145 rate is £20–35 below a set ranging from £165 to £180. That is real evidence there is room to raise prices, and it is the strongest argument in the paper.
- **Sell-outs.** Selling out on 31 Saturdays means demand exceeded supply on those nights, which also supports higher prices at peak times.
- **Monitoring.** Comparing against the same weeks in 2025 is the right baseline because it removes seasonality.

## Main problems

**1. The price "test" is the summer season, not a price effect.** June 2025 was 81% and July was 89%. But Table 1 shows that July and August are the hotel's strongest months every year because of the harbour festival and school holidays. June itself was a dip from May's 85%. A seasonal rise of that size would have happened at any price.

Two further problems:
- **Booking timing.** Many July stays would already have been booked before the rate changed in the last week of June, so the rise largely couldn't have affected them.
- **Missing comparison.** The relevant test is July 2025 against July 2024, which the paper doesn't give.

The data cannot show that guests are "not price sensitive," and the idea that the rise "reinforced our positioning" has no support.

**2. The value-for-money score was measured at the old, cheaper price.** An 8.4 score at £145, the cheapest in the set, partly reflects being cheapest. It says little about how guests will rate value at £165, where the hotel moves from cheapest to level with the cheapest competitor.

**3. The revenue estimate is not a floor.**

| Issue | Effect |
|---|---|
| Room count: Section 2 says 112 rooms, Section 5 uses 124 | £204k falls to about **£184k** at 112 |
| Not every room sells at BAR: wedding blocks (38% of Saturdays), contracted group and corporate rates, and packages are unaffected | roughly a fifth or more of weekend room-nights won't see the £20 |
| OTA commission (typically 15–20%) on rooms sold through online agents | each £20 yields less than £20 |
| VAT: UK consumer room rates are normally quoted including VAT, while room revenue is normally reported net | £20 gross is £16.67 net |

The illustrative estimate below makes some assumptions: wedding blocks are about a fifth of weekend room-nights, other contracted rates are ignored, VAT is removed, and there is some OTA commission. On that basis the realistic gain, before any loss in volume, is roughly **£110–150k**, not "at least £204k." The finance team can tighten this with the actual channel mix.

**4. The two-night minimum is aimed at the wrong guests and may lose Saturday nights.** Section 4 says wedding guests are 38% of Saturday bookings and stay exactly one night, Saturday to Sunday. Already-contracted groups are protected, but weddings booked from June onwards would face the minimum. Couples planning blocks may simply send guests to a hotel without one.

More generally, a guest who wants one Saturday night may book elsewhere rather than pay for two. On the 21 Saturdays that didn't sell out, the restriction mostly turns business away. On the 31 that did, it may convert some guests to two nights or it may lose them.

So the minimum has both an upside and a downside, and neither is quantified. That means £204k is not a floor, as the author's description claims. Standard practice is to apply a minimum stay only on dates forecast to sell out, and to exempt or price wedding blocks separately.

**5. The rate rise probably pays for itself, but not because demand is insensitive.** The rise is 13.8% (£165 / £145). Room revenue only falls if weekend occupancy drops by more than about 12% in relative terms, from 79% to around 69.5%, or roughly 9–10 points. Losses on food and drink from fewer guests narrow that margin somewhat. That buffer, together with the competitor gap, is the honest argument for the rise, and it is a fairly good one.

## Smaller points

- **Flat rate across the year.** A flat £165 treats January (62%) the same as August (93%). A seasonal or demand-based structure is likely to earn more with less risk: higher rates from July to September and on sell-out Saturdays, more caution from January to March.
- **Monitoring.**
  - The five-point trigger is sensible, and well inside the break-even margin, but "review the rate" names no action.
  - Occupancy alone won't show what the two-night minimum is doing. The hotel should also track denied Saturday enquiries, wedding-block enquiries lost, and Friday and Sunday pick-up.
  - The weekly pick-up review would catch problems sooner than the monthly figures that the author's description relies on.
- **Recommendation wording.** "The evidence shows … not price sensitive" should be removed. The evidence does not show it.

## Suggested changes

1. Correct the room count, and estimate revenue only on BAR-sold room-nights, net of VAT and commission. Show the break-even occupancy alongside it.
2. Replace the June-to-July comparison with year-on-year data, or drop it and rest the case on the competitor gap and the break-even margin.
3. Restrict the two-night minimum to forecast sell-out dates, and decide how wedding blocks are treated before it goes live.
4. Consider seasonal pricing rather than a flat £165.

The £20 rise is defensible. What should go to the owners is an expected gain of perhaps £110–150k with clear downside risks, not a guaranteed minimum of £204k.
